newsitem.title: UK: Turtles follow straight and narrow, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Turtles follow straight and narrow, study finds.

text.p: Migrating leatherback turtles follow clearly defined and very narrow paths when migrating, U.S. scientists reported on Wednesday.
Stephen Morreale of Cornell University and colleagues said their findings were important not only to efforts to save the endangered turtles, but to anyone studying the delicate ecology of the ocean.
They tracked eight female leatherback turtles which had laid eggs in Costa Rica as they swam via the Galapagos islands into deeper Pacific waters.
Using satellite telemetry, they discovered a clear route used by turtles in their annual migration.

"As the turtle rises to the surface to breathe, the attached transmitter sends a signal to a satellite, which calculates and relays the location of the animal," they wrote in a letter to the scientific journal Nature.

Because it is hard to attach a transmitter directly to leatherback turtles, which can dive to 1,000 metres (3,200 ft) they invented a hydrodynamic one that could trail behind the animals as they swam.

Some of them were tracked for 2,700 km (1,700 miles) and showed remarkable patterns. "Turtles within the same season travelled along similar, and in some cases virtually identical, pathways," they wrote.

"In 1992, two turtles were located within 20 km (12 miles) of each other after 37 days and more than 700 km (435 miles) from the nesting beach, even though they left the beach 13 days apart," they wrote.
"Over the four consecutive years of our study, the tracks of all eight turtles were within a relatively narrow corridor extending southwestwards into the open Pacific."
They said they did not know how the turtles stuck to such a narrow path but it could have something to do with currents or available food.
